Cercospora.name: Cercospora
Cercospora.description: A fungal disease causing brown eye spot or Cercospora leaf spot on coffee plants. The pathogen produces cercosporin, a photoactivated toxin that damages leaf tissue. Favored by warm, humid conditions (20-28C with 36-72 hours of continuous wetness).
symptoms: Chlorotic (yellow) spots that expand into deep brown necrotic lesions
Light-colored centers where sporulation occurs
Yellow halo around lesion margins caused by cercosporin toxin
Lesions may fuse to form large irregular areas of necrotic tissue
Leaf drop in extreme cases
management_practices: Prune branches to improve air circulation and reduce leaf wetness
Maintain balanced soil nutrition (avoid both deficiency and excess nitrogen)
Ensure proper drainage to minimize humidity
Apply copper-based fungicides during flowering and dry weather
Space plants adequately (e.g., 8 ft x 8 ft) to reduce plant stress
Cercospora.ethiopian_context: Literature suggests Cercospora is not a significant problem in Ethiopia and Uganda, Africa's top coffee-producing countries. However, monitoring is still recommended as climate conditions change.
citations: Nelson, S. (2008). Cercospora Leaf Spot and Berry Blotch of Coffee. University of Hawaii at Manoa, CTAHR.
Gaitan, A.L. (2015). Compendium of Coffee Diseases and Pests. APS Press. pp. 27-28.
Waller, J.M., Bigger, M., Hillocks, R.J. (2007). Coffee Pests, Diseases & Their Management. CABI.

Healthy.name: Healthy
Healthy.description: No disease symptoms detected on the leaf. The leaf shows normal coloration and tissue integrity without lesions, spots, pustules, or mining patterns.
symptoms: Uniform green leaf coloration
No lesions, spots, or discoloration
No powdery growths or pustules on either leaf surface
No tunneling or mining patterns visible
Normal leaf turgor and texture
management_practices: Continue regular monitoring for early disease detection
Maintain balanced nutrition, particularly nitrogen and potassium
Ensure proper plant spacing and pruning for air circulation
Manage shade levels appropriate to the growing region
Implement integrated pest management practices
Healthy.ethiopian_context: Ethiopia is the birthplace of Coffea arabica. Healthy coffee plants in Ethiopia's highland regions (1,500-2,200m elevation) benefit from the cool, misty conditions, but climate change is increasing disease pressure.
citations: Tadesse, T. et al. (2020). Coffee production constraints and opportunities at major growing districts of southern Ethiopia. Cogent Food & Agriculture.
Kew Royal Botanic Gardens. Building a climate resilient coffee economy for Ethiopia.

Leaf Rust.name: Leaf Rust
Leaf Rust.description: Coffee leaf rust (CLR) is one of the most economically important coffee diseases worldwide. The fungus reduces the plant's photosynthetic ability by covering leaves with spores and causing defoliation. The pathogen is believed to have East African origin. Optimal development occurs at 16-28C with free water on leaves.
symptoms: Yellow-orange powdery pustules on the underside of leaves
Chlorotic or pale yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Lesions expand from small points (~0.1mm) to several centimeters
Defoliation in severe infections
Reduced flower and fruit production
management_practices: Plant resistant cultivars where available (most effective long-term strategy)
Apply copper-based fungicides such as Bordeaux mixture as preventative treatment
Prune to improve air circulation and reduce leaf wetness
Maintain adequate nitrogen and potassium nutrition for plant resistance
Remove infected leaves to reduce inoculum
Increase spacing between rows to improve air circulation
Leaf Rust.ethiopian_context: Coffee leaf rust is believed to have originated in the highlands of Ethiopia, Sudan, and Kenya. It was first reported in the 1860s from Kenya. As climate change increases temperatures and alters rainfall patterns in Ethiopia, rust pressure is expected to increase.
citations: Talhinhas, P. et al. (2017). The coffee leaf rust pathogen Hemileia vastatrix: one and a half centuries around the tropics. Molecular Plant Pathology 18(8): 1039-1051.
Kushalappa, A.C. (2017). Coffee Rust. CRC Press.
Waller, J.M., Bigger, M., Hillocks, R.J. (2007). Coffee Pests, Diseases & Their Management. CABI.

Miner.name: Miner
Miner.description: The coffee leaf miner is a moth whose larvae feed on coffee leaf tissue, creating characteristic tunnels or mines. It is considered one of the worst pest species of coffee in the Americas. The adult moth has a wingspan of approximately 6.5mm.
symptoms: Visible tunnels or mines in the leaf tissue
Brown or discolored serpentine patterns on the leaf surface
Damaged leaf areas may turn brown and necrotic
Reduced photosynthetic capacity in heavily mined leaves
Leaf drop in severe infestations
management_practices: Monitor populations regularly to detect early infestations
Encourage natural predators such as social wasps (Protonectarina sylveirae, Synoeca cyanea)
Apply targeted insecticide only when pest thresholds are exceeded
Remove and destroy heavily infested leaves
Maintain field sanitation to reduce overwintering sites
Miner.ethiopian_context: Coffee leaf miner is primarily reported as a major problem in the Americas. In Ethiopia, monitoring is recommended as pest ranges may shift with changing climate conditions.
citations: Fernandes, F.L. et al. (2013). Selectivity of old and new organophosphate insecticides and behavior of Vespidae predators in coffee crop. Sociobiology 60(4): 471-476.
Waller, J.M., Bigger, M., Hillocks, R.J. (2007). Coffee Pests, Diseases & Their Management. CABI.

Phoma.name: Phoma
Phoma.description: A soil fungus that infects the leaves and fruits of coffee plants prior to fruit ripening. Less extensively documented than other coffee diseases, but can cause significant damage under favorable conditions.
symptoms: Lesions on leaves and developing fruits
Infection occurs before fruit ripening
Sunken, discolored spots on affected tissue
May lead to berry drop in severe cases
management_practices: Implement cultural practices including proper plant spacing
Remove and destroy infected plant material
Ensure adequate air circulation through pruning
Avoid excessive moisture around the base of plants
Monitor soil health and drainage conditions
Phoma.ethiopian_context: Specific data on Phoma incidence in Ethiopian coffee is limited. General cultural management practices are recommended, and monitoring should be maintained as part of integrated disease management.
citations: Echandi, E. (1957). Original species description of Phoma costaricensis.
Novtahaning, D. et al. (2022). Deep Learning Ensemble-Based Automated and High-Performing Recognition of Coffee Leaf Disease. Agriculture 12(11): 1909.
Gaitan, A.L. (2015). Compendium of Coffee Diseases and Pests. APS Press.
